ch01.note: Tianbao (742–756) was the third and last reign-era of Emperor Xuanzong. From 744 its years were styled zai (载) rather than the usual nian (年), an archaizing usage the court adopted for the era; so the source’s 天宝三载 is ‘the third year of Tianbao,’ that is 744 CE. The fourteenth of the first lunar month falls in early spring.

ch01.anchor: the hour of the Snake, second half
ch01.note: The traditional day ran in twelve shichen, each equal to two modern hours and named for the twelve earthly branches and their zodiac animals. Each shichen divided into a first half (chu, 初) and a second half (zheng, 正); the Snake’s second half (si zheng, 巳正) centers on 10 a.m. The novel’s twenty-four chapters are the twenty-four half-shichen of one day, and each chapter is named for the hour it covers.

The Lantern Festival (Shangyuan, 上元) falls on the fifteenth night of the first lunar month; the chapter opens on its eve, the fourteenth. For its nights the capital’s strict curfew was suspended and the wards were hung with lanterns—the one season when Chang'an’s people could move freely after dark, and so the natural cover for the plot the Bureau fears.

The Sogdians were the Iranian merchant people of Central Asia who dominated Silk Road trade. Kang (康) was their city-state of Samarkand, chief among the ‘Nine Surnames of Zhaowu’ whose emigrants to China took surnames from their home cities—Cao, Kang, An, Shi, and the rest. The surname Cao thus marks the traveler, by his cover at least, as one of them.

A guosuo (过所) was the official permit required to move goods and persons through the empire’s checkpoints. It recorded the bearer, his party, and his cargo, and had to be inspected and sealed at every barrier along the road; to forge or misuse one was a grave offense.

ch01.anchor: a gold fish-pouch at his waist
ch01.note: Officials of the fifth rank and above wore a fish-shaped tally in a pouch at the belt as a badge of rank—gold for the third rank and up, silver below. The elder’s gold pouch marks a senior man; the young deputy’s silver one, as the narration later notes, is a grant from the emperor above his own sixth rank, a visible token of special favor.

The fly-whisk (fuchen, 拂尘) is a Daoist ritual implement; in the hand of an administrative officer it is incongruous, and it marks the young official’s Daoist bent. The historical Li Bi was famous for his Daoism and for repeatedly withdrawing to the mountains to practice it.

ch01.anchor: from the hand of Yan Zhenqing
ch01.note: Yan Zhenqing (709–785) was one of the supreme masters of Chinese calligraphy, his regular script celebrated for its full, upright strength. A real historical figure of the age; that the new Bureau’s name-board should be in his hand marks both its standing and its recent founding.

Özmiş Qaghan (r. 742–744) was the last ruler of the Second Turkic Khaganate. Historically a coalition of the Basmyl, Uyghurs, and Karluks broke his power and killed him in 744—the very year in which the novel is set—and his head was sent to the Tang court. The book’s frontier backdrop is thus genuine history; the account here is corroborated by the Tang annals.

The anecdote is drawn from the historical Li Bi’s biography: brought before Xuanzong as a boy prodigy, he capped the minister Zhang Yue’s verse on the chessboard and was rewarded with a place in the heir apparent’s study. Recorded in the Tang histories; corroborated. Li Bi (722–789) went on to serve four emperors as one of the dynasty’s most celebrated statesmen.

Zimei (子美) was the courtesy name of the poet Du Fu (712–770), who was living in and around Chang'an in just these years. The drunkard, taking the fleeing Cao Poyan for a friend, hails him by that name—a quiet authorial wink that the English can only footnote. Corroborated: Du Fu’s zi was indeed Zimei.

‘The Sage’ (shengren, 圣人) was a Tang court term of address for the reigning emperor, here Xuanzong (r. 712–756). The elder’s guarded phrase a moment later—‘that person,’ with a nod toward the palace—means the same man.

ch02.note: He Zhizhang (659–744) was a celebrated Tang poet and official who served as Director of the Palace Library (Taichangqing / Secretary-General of the Imperial Clan Court, then Mishujian). A friend of Li Bai, he was famous for his poetry, his love of wine, and his nickname ‘the Drunken Sage of the Four Wisdoms.’ He retired to become a Daoist priest in 744, the very year the novel is set, and died shortly after. That the novel makes him the Jing’an Bureau’s nominal head is an invention—but his post as jian (Director) and his presence in Chang’an in early 744 are historical. Corroborated: biography in the Old Book of Tang and New Book of Tang.

Suluk (Çor) Khagan (r. 716–738) was the ruler of the Türgesh, a Western Turkic tribal confederation based in the Chu and Ili river valleys. He was a formidable adversary of both the Tang and the Umayyad Caliphate. The siege of Balhuan (拨换城, near modern Aksu in Xinjiang) is recorded in the Tang histories under the year 735 (Kaiyuan 23). The historical Gai Jiayun served as Protector-General of Beiting and did relieve the siege, though the novel embellishes the details. Suluk was assassinated by his own general Baga Tarkhan in 738. Corroborated: Zizhi Tongjian, juan 214; P. B. Golden, An Introduction to the History of the Turkic Peoples.

Cen Shen (岑参, c. 715–770) was one of the great Tang frontier poets, celebrated for his vivid depictions of the Western Regions. He was indeed from a family registered in Xianzhou (modern Nanyang, Henan). In 744 he would have been about twenty-nine, a young man not yet famous—his horse-and-poems cameo here is an authorial wink much like the Du Fu appearance in Chapter One. His first-person indignation at the burning of his verse is a charming irony, since the poems that survive made him immortal. Corroborated: standard biographical sources; see S. Owen, The Great Age of Chinese Poetry: The High T’ang.

ch03.note: The sabao (萨宝; from a Sogdian/Middle Persian title for a caravan leader) was a real Tang office: the government-recognized headman of a resident foreign—chiefly Sogdian—community, who also had charge of its Zoroastrian temples and priests. The Sabao Office (萨宝府) administered such communities under loose imperial oversight, which is why the novel’s Great Sabao can both speak for the believers and be leaned on by the court. Corroborated: the office is attested in Tang institutional sources and in the epitaphs of Sogdian sabao in China.

ch03.anchor: Eight Immortals of the Wine Cup
ch03.note: The ‘Eight Immortals of the Wine Cup’ (饮中八仙) are eight celebrated Tang drinkers immortalized in Du Fu’s poem Song of the Eight Immortals of the Wine Cup: He Zhizhang, Li Bai, Li Shizhi, Li Jin (Prince of Ruyang), Cui Zongzhi, Su Jin, Zhang Xu, and Jiao Sui—of whom Jiao Sui alone held no office. Du Fu’s poem opens with He Zhizhang, so the novel’s placing him ‘at their head’ follows the poem. Corroborated: the roster is Du Fu’s; all eight are historical figures of Xuanzong’s reign.

The Pingkang li (平康里), a ward in the northeast of Chang'an close to the imperial city and the examination offices, was the capital’s famous pleasure district, where the registered courtesans lived. It was divided into three lanes (曲); the northern lane—here called the First Lane—was the humblest, frequented by commoners and struggling examination candidates. Corroborated: described in Sun Qi’s late-Tang Beili zhi (北里志, ‘Record of the Northern Ward’).

‘Kunlun slave’ (昆倬奴) was the Tang term for dark-skinned servants brought from the southern seas and beyond; they are stock figures of Tang tales, most famously in the chuanqi story The Kunlun Slave. Old Ge is later specified as a sengqi slave (僵祁奴), that is a Zanj—from the Arabic name for the East African coast—such enslaved Africans reaching Tang China by way of Arab and Persian traders. Corroborated: both terms are attested in Tang sources; see E. H. Schafer, The Golden Peaches of Samarkand.

ch04.note: Xun Yue (148–209) was a Later Han historian and political thinker; his Shenjian (申鉴, ‘Extended Reflections’), presented to Emperor Xian, is a treatise of statecraft. The maxim Li Bi quotes—fang wei shang, jiu ci zhi (防为上，救次之), ‘prevention comes first, remedy second’—is genuinely from it. Corroborated: the line stands in the received Shenjian.

ch04.anchor: the burning house of the Buddhist scriptures
ch04.note: An allusion to the Parable of the Burning House in the Lotus Sutra: children play on heedless inside a blazing mansion until their father lures them out with the promise of splendid carts. In Buddhist usage the ‘burning house’ (huozhai, 火宅) is the whole world of suffering, from which the Buddha draws sentient beings; the image turns the pavilion’s literal fire into a figure for that peril.

The Five Kennels (wu fang, 五坊) were the five palace establishments that kept the emperor’s hunting birds and hounds: eagles, gyrfalcons, hawks, sparrowhawks, and dogs. A real Tang institution; their keepers, the ‘Five Kennels boys’ (wufang xiao’er), grew notorious in the ninth century for extorting the people under cover of requisitioning feed for the birds. Corroborated: attested in the Tang histories and satirized in Bai Juyi’s New Music Bureau poems.

ch05.note: Li Lin (李琳, d. 757), Prince Yong, was a son of Emperor Xuanzong. History remembers him not for polo but for his end: after the An Lushan rebellion he was given a great command in the southeast, and in 757 raised troops along the Yangtze in what the court branded a revolt; he was defeated and killed. The poet Li Bai, who had joined his staff, was arrested and exiled for the association. Corroborated: biographies in the Old Book of Tang and New Book of Tang. The novel’s petty, queasy prince is thus a real historical figure seen years before his ruin.

A quiet stroke of dramatic irony. Yuan Zai (元载, d. 777) is here a forgettable eighth-rank Evaluator whose very name Prince Yong can barely recall—yet history made him the husband of Wang Yunxiu, the same Wang Zhongsi’s daughter whose abduction drives this day’s events, and then a chief minister under Emperor Daizong, one of the most notoriously corrupt of the dynasty, executed for his greed in 777. Corroborated: the marriage and career are recorded in the Tang histories; the poem-exchange of Yuan Zai and Wang Yunxiu was long famous.

Polo (jiju) was a ruling passion of the Tang court, and its grounds were watered—or, for the rich, oiled—to lay the dust, whence this field’s name. It is a historical site: Yang Shenjiao (杨慎交), husband of Princess Changning, a daughter of Emperor Zhongzong, was recorded as sprinkling his polo ground with oil, a byword for their household’s extravagance. Corroborated: the anecdote stands in the New Book of Tang and the Zizhi Tongjian.

ch06.note: The novel’s shizhi (石脂, literally ‘stone-grease’) is petroleum—the naphtha that seeps to the surface in the northwest. The detail that Yanzhou (modern Yan’an) petroleum was burned for its soot to make a prized ink is genuine history: the Song polymath Shen Kuo, who coined the very word shiyou (石油, ‘rock-oil,’ still the modern Chinese for petroleum), records in his Dream Pool Essays that he made ink from Yan’an petroleum-soot and judged it finer than pine-soot ink. Corroborated.

Menghuo (狩火, ‘fierce-fire’) and its bomb the menghuo lei are the novel’s version of the naphtha incendiary that real Tang and Song armies called menghuoyou (狩火油, ‘fierce-fire oil’)—the distilled-petroleum weapon that reached China from the eastern Mediterranean, kin to Byzantine ‘Greek fire.’ Its use, and purpose-built pump-projectors for it, are described in the Song military compendium Wujing Zongyao (1044). The clinging, unquenchable flame Zhang Xiaojing describes is just what the sources report. Corroborated—though the sealed bursting-jar ‘thunder’ is the author’s own extrapolation.

Jiajie (假节, literally ‘to be lent the tally’) was a real institution of the Han and the Wei-Jin period: the emperor delegated a portion of his own authority to a general or governor by conferring a tally (jie, 节), which carried defined powers of command and of summary punishment. The novel borrows the ancient term for the Jing’an Bureau’s device of routing every watchtower’s reports to a single field commander—a fictional usage, but the text’s gloss of the words (jia = to lend, jie = authority) is faithful to the historical term.
